Vietnam during the spread of communism

It did not begin here. The Americans were advised to resist in this manner — by advisers, by money, by a client government, and not by an army of their own — and the adviser was Dwight D. Eisenhower, in April 1954, when he refused the air strike at Dien Bien Phu and chose instead to build a South. Everything the four presidents managed afterward was the working-out of that manner of resistance.

Communism, as an idea

1848Marx and Engels, the Manifesto: class struggle, the abolition of private property in the means of production, the workers of the world.
1917Lenin: a vanguard party seizes a state and holds it. The idea acquires an army and a capital.
1919The Comintern: the idea exported, with instructions. Anti-colonial nationalists are told that their enemy is the same as the workers’ enemy.
1920Nguyen Ai Quoc — Ho Chi Minh — votes at Tours to found the French Communist Party, because it was the one party that would talk about Indochina.
1930The Indochinese Communist Party founded in Hong Kong. The idea now has a Vietnamese branch, and the branch is also the national movement.
1941The Viet Minh: a communist-led front that fights Japan and then France, and is armed for a season by the American OSS.
1946Kennan’s Long Telegram: the idea is expansive and must be contained. Containment becomes the American answer, and Vietnam becomes a place where it is applied.
1949China goes communist; Mao recognises Ho in January 1950; Truman recognises Bao Dai a month later and starts paying France’s war.
1950NSC-68: any loss anywhere is a loss everywhere. Korea, that June, seems to prove it.
1954The domino theory, in Eisenhower’s words, on 7 April. Dien Bien Phu falls on 7 May. Geneva divides the country at the 17th parallel, temporarily.
1960The Sino-Soviet split. The idea now has two capitals that dislike each other, both of which arm Hanoi, each to outdo the other. Washington reads this slowly.
1975Saigon falls. The dominoes that fall are Cambodia and Laos; Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia and the Philippines do not, and in 1979 communist Vietnam and communist China go to war with each other.

Who funded communism, and why are its ideas traced back further?

Marx, 1849–1883Friedrich Engels, from the profits of Ermen & Engels, his family’s cotton mill in Manchester. Marx lived for thirty years largely on Engels’s money and Engels finished Capital after he died. The bank behind the idea was a textile firm and a friend.
The ideas, before MarxHegel for the dialectic; Ricardo and Smith for the labour theory of value; Saint-Simon, Fourier, Owen and Babeuf for socialism; Rousseau for the critique of property. Common ownership itself is traced back further still, and honestly — Plato’s guardians, the Acts of the Apostles, Müntzer in 1525, Winstanley’s Diggers in 1649 — which is why the idea cannot be pinned to one funder: it was old before anyone paid for it.
Lenin, 1917The German Imperial government, through Alexander Parvus and the Foreign Office, financed Bolshevik propaganda and arranged the sealed train from Zürich in April 1917, to take Russia out of the war. The sum is disputed; the fact is documented in the German archives. Germany funded its own defeat in 1918 by the same means.
The parties abroad, 1919–1943The Comintern, from the Soviet state: confiscated gold and jewels at first, budget later. Ho Chi Minh was a Comintern agent on its payroll in the 1920s and 1930s.
Hanoi, 1950–1975China from 1950, the Soviet Union from the late 1950s, each outbidding the other after the split: about $2 billion a year in Soviet aid by the end, and Chinese troops keeping the railways open under the bombing.
The mythThat a hidden syndicate of bankers — the names usually given are Schiff, Warburg, Rothschild — funded the Bolsheviks. This is false and it is the Protocols of the Elders of Zion in another coat. Jacob Schiff funded the Provisional Government of Kerensky and denounced the Bolsheviks; the Warburgs lost their Russian interests to them. The claim was spread by White émigrés in 1919 and by Henry Ford in 1920 and has no documentary basis. It is named here so it cannot be mistaken for the row above it.
Incognito. Why is a hidden syndicate bad? In this repository the answer is technical and it is the same one lesson four gives: a checkpoint you cannot recompute is a claim, not a proof, and a syndicate whose doors are hidden cannot be audited by its neighbours, so nothing it carries can be trusted at the interval. In history the answer is the mirror of that: a claim that a hidden syndicate is behind an event cannot be recomputed either, which is exactly why such claims are made. An unfalsifiable funder is the shape a libel takes. See project 34.

Three lenses

Our war room

The room is American and it is in this repository: the chain of five presidents, the gauge of troops by year, the line fitted to the provinces lost. It sees decisions. It does not see Hanoi’s Politburo, which had a room of its own with a longer horizon, or Saigon’s palace, which had the least say of the three.

The war theatre

Indochina, not Vietnam: the Ho Chi Minh Trail ran through Laos and Cambodia, the air bases were in Thailand, the B-52s flew from Guam and Okinawa, the fleet sat at Yankee Station, and the treaty was signed in Paris. Twenty-seven nations appear in the table; the fighting touched four countries and the bombing three.

The war itself

Depending on where the count starts, it was thirty years (1945, the August Revolution), twenty (1955, the American date), or ten (1965, the Marines). For the Vietnamese it was one war with several foreigners in it — Japan, France, the United States, then China in 1979 — and the idea, communism, was the vehicle of a nationalism older than any of them. That is what the American room could not see from inside: it was containing an idea, and fighting a nation.

Why was the Holocaust reclassified, and compared to communism’s dead?

1986, the HistorikerstreitErnst Nolte argued in the FAZ that the Gulag was the “original” and Auschwitz a reaction to it; Habermas and most German historians replied that this relativised a crime that was singular in kind — the industrial murder of a people for being born — and that comparison was being used to excuse. The argument was about whether the Holocaust could be filed as one atrocity among the century’s, and the answer of the profession was no.
1997, The Black Book of CommunismCourtois’s introduction put communism’s dead at about 100 million and compared the class terror to the racial one. The book’s own contributors, Werth and Margolin, objected to the introduction; the figure was contested and the comparison became a political standard for the post-Soviet right.
2008–2019, the declarationsThe Prague Declaration (2008) and the European Parliament’s resolution of September 2019 treated Nazi and Stalinist crimes as equivalent and set 23 August as a joint day of remembrance. Baltic and Polish governments pushed it as recognition of their own dead; Jewish organisations and many historians objected that “double genocide” was being used in places to obscure local collaboration in the Holocaust.
What the comparison is forComparison is what history does; equation is what politics does with it. Both regimes killed by category; only one built factories for it and hunted infants across a continent for what their grandparents were. The Vietnamese count in this room, 1.4 to 3.8 million, is not on either side of that argument, and it is the number this repository is actually about.
